transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I’ve been feeling like the best part of my life is already behind me. It’s not dramatic, exactly, but it’s a stubborn feeling that no matter how much I plan or try to get disciplined, I’m not going to get back to feeling like myself.
How long have you been feeling this way—has it been a few weeks, or more like months to years?
It’s been more like years. It started after my hiking injury—so, a little over three years ago now, about three years and three months.
Over these three years, has this low, discouraged feeling been present nearly every day, or have there been stretches of weeks or months where you felt essentially back to your normal self?
Nearly every day, I think. I’m not crying or anything like that, but there’s this low, gray feeling underneath everything—even when I’m in the studio or having dinner with my wife.

During these past three years, has there ever been a stretch of two weeks or more where your mood or energy dropped noticeably lower than this usual baseline—like a distinct worsening—or has it stayed at about the same level the whole time?
I’m not really sure. It’s mostly felt like the same low level for so long that I don’t know I could point to a separate stretch where it was clearly worse.
Along with this low mood, have you also noticed changes in your sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, or self-worth that occur together, nearly every day, for two weeks or more at a time?

Yes—the fatigue is pretty constant. I still get up and do the shopping and work on little projects, but even setting up for a mentoring session or walking through a community event can leave me worn out. A nap doesn’t really seem to fix it.
Over these past three years, have you often felt a sense of hopelessness about things getting better?

Yes. It’s a quiet kind of hopelessness, but it’s there. I’ve started to feel like the best part of my life may already be behind me, and that no amount of planning or discipline is going to get me back to feeling like myself.
Over these past three years, have you noticed a consistent change in your sleep—either trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping much more than usual?
I’m not sure I’ve noticed a consistent change in my sleep, no.
Over these past three years, have you noticed a consistent change in your appetite—either eating much less or much more than usual?
I haven’t really noticed a consistent change in my appetite.
Over these past three years, have you noticed ongoing trouble concentrating or making decisions, even about everyday things?
I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed an ongoing problem with concentrating or making everyday decisions.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a chronic, low-grade depressive mood present nearly every day for over three years following a physical injury, without a clear superimposed major depressive episode (no distinct two-week period of worsening mood, no sleep or appetite disturbance, no concentration difficulty). Accompanying symptoms include persistent fatigue and quiet hopelessness about the future, consistent with at least two associated symptoms required for dysthymia. The chronicity (>2 years), absence of symptom-free intervals longer than two months, and subthreshold severity (not meeting full major depressive episode criteria) support a diagnosis of Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia, F34.1) rather than Major Depressive Disorder or an adjustment disorder, given the stressor occurred years prior and symptoms have persisted well beyond typical adjustment disorder duration.
